relations.note: Loko and Ayizan are conventionally husband and wife and priestly counterparts.
relations.source: Marcelin, Métraux, and later Haitian ethnography

relations.note: They jointly protect initiation, ritual purity, and priestly transmission.
relations.source: Marcelin, Métraux, and later Haitian ethnography

relations.note: Loko lived in Ayizan's house, revolted, and departed to assume a separate domain.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: A Rara performance salutes Legba and then Papa Loko.

relations.myth: Ayizan walks with Legba and Loko
relations.note: Marcelin places Legba and Loko together as companions of Ayizan.
Loko and Danbala Wedo are greeted together in an initiation sequence.
Danbala and Loko join the divine exodus from Ayizan's household.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Ezili Freda and Loko depart Ayizan's household during the same revolt.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Agwe and Loko depart Ayizan's household and assume separate domains.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Zaka and Loko depart Ayizan's household during the same divine exodus.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Loko joins the departing group for which Sobo makes a signal flag.
relations.source: Vodou in Haitian Life and Culture

relations.note: Loko is classified as a later child or member of the Mawu-Lisa pantheon.
Huntin and Loko are jointly invoked as agencies for causing another's death.
Fon Loko and Yoruba Ìrókò are compared or equated as corresponding sacred-tree powers.
Joseph's image and feast serve as Loko's Catholic counterpart in Haitian practice.
